book_context: Late in the book, after an omitted chapter of travel and silence, Adams reaches sixty while his closest friends hold power. John Hay is ambassador in London and then Secretary of State; Lodge is a Senator; Roosevelt follows. Clarence King and Hay are declining. The recurring mechanisms carry forward: 'a friend in power is a friend lost'; sitting on the steps of Ara Coeli; Pteraspis, Lyell and Limulus from the Darwinism chapter; women and the Virgin as force; and the search for unity against multiplicity, now recast as attempts to measure history mechanically. These chapters move from diplomatic triumph to the dynamo and the Virgin, then to magnets, geology and Russian inertia. They prepare the formal 'Dynamic Theory' and the 'Law of Acceleration'. Omitted chapters (Chicago, Silence, Grant, Eccentricity) leave some setup that must be glossed locally: Hay sent to London; the dynamos first seen at Chicago in 1893.

essential: Adams haunts the 1900 Exposition helplessly until Langley strips it to its forces. Bacon taught as much in 1620, but literary knowledge was useless without application. Note briefly that his study of force began at Chicago in 1893.
Langley throws out art and industry and teaches motors and automobiles. The automobile has become a nightmare since 1893 and the locomotive is almost Adams's own age.

The hall of dynamos. To Langley the dynamo is a channel for coal-heat; to Adams it becomes a symbol of infinity, a moral force like the Cross, quieter than the planet, and finally something to pray to.
There is a break of continuity between steam and electricity. Langley calls the new rays anarchical and parricidal: radium denied its God.
A 'Paradise of ignorance': the new forces (Branly coherer, X-rays) are incapable of expression in horse-power. A supersensual universe; 'physics stark mad in metaphysics'.

Historians' unconscious assumptions of cause and effect. His own dozen volumes failed to fix sequence. He moves through the sequences of men, society, time and thought, then turns to force. Historical neck broken.
Comparison to 1500 and 1600, with the nearest parallel 310 and Constantine's Cross. The rays as 'immediate modes of the divine substance'.
Method: reduce forces to their attraction on his own mind, and translate rays into faith. The Boston chemist could feel both, though the rays were unborn and the women dead.

The Virgin and Venus as force in France (Lourdes, Chartres) but only sentiment in America; fig-leaves; Puritan sex-as-sin. Keep the Lucretius line 'Quae quondam rerum naturam sola gubernas' paired with the Dante invocation, at least in part.
American art is sexless; only Whitman, Bret Harte and a few painters treated sex as force. He cared nothing for the sex of the dynamo until he could measure its energy.

St. Gaudens: inarticulate and simple. At Amiens, Gibbon's 'contemptuous look' and Ruskin show that one sees what one brings. St. Gaudens loved the monuments but did not feel the Virgin's force; Renaissance soul in an American cradle; the horse as his symbol of power.

Both energies act on man and can be measured by that action; the Virgin as the greatest force the West felt. The pursuit into scholastic thickets; the pen as blind man's dog, with results depending on what is struck out; sailing from Cherbourg, January 19, 1901.

voice_profile: Third-person autobiography in which the elderly Adams treats his younger and present self with ironic detachment ('Adams', 'one', 'the student', 'the tourist', 'an insect', 'the monkey'). Long periodic sentences turn on qualification and paradox. Cosmic science metaphors (force, mass, inertia, triangulation, attraction) are applied to politics and friendship. He undercuts himself constantly through self-deprecation and mock-pedantry. He flatly refuses certainty ('knew no more than...'). Aphoristic closers end paragraphs. Foreign tags and verse quotations act as punctuation. Grief appears only obliquely, through restraint and stage-images. Double hyphens mark interruption and accumulation.
